extracted.intended_audience: systematic review authors and meta-analysts (especially Cochrane review authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting and interpreting meta-analyses in intervention systematic reviews, covering choice of effect measures for different outcome types, handling data features (skew, change scores, mixed outcome formats), and assessment and management of heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of normal distribution for continuous outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard meta-analysis methods for continuous data assume outcomes are approximately normally distributed in each intervention arm in each study; this may not hold especially in small studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware this assumption is unimportant in very large studies but can be problematic in small trials; consider skew and alternative approaches (see Section 10.5.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of summary statistic for continuous outcomes (MD, SMD, ratio of means)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select mean difference (MD) when studies report the outcome on the same scale, standardized mean difference (SMD) when studies use different scales, and ratio of means when outcomes are strictly greater than zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also consider interpretability (see Chapter 15). The choice should be driven by scale comparability and practical interpretability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand role of standard deviations in MD approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mean difference approach, study SDs and sample sizes determine study weights; studies with small SDs receive relatively higher weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This weighting is appropriate only if between-study SD differences reflect measurement reliability rather than true population variability. Bear this assumption in mind if SDs vary unexpectedly across studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand role of standard deviations in SMD approach
rubrics_metrics.description: In the standardized mean difference approach, SDs are used both to standardize mean differences and to compute study weights; studies with small SDs produce larger SMD estimates and receive relatively higher weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate only if between-study variation in SDs reflects differences in measurement scales (not differences in reliability or population variability). Be cautious when SDs vary for substantive reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer adjusted analyses for baseline (ANCOVA) over naive change scores
rubrics_metrics.description: The preferred statistical approach to account for baseline measurements is to include baseline outcome measurements as a covariate in a regression model or ANCOVA, yielding adjusted estimates and standard errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These adjusted estimates are most precise and least biased and should be included when available; they can only be included using the generic inverse-variance method because group means and SDs are not available separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of change-from-baseline versus post-intervention values (MD)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using unstandardized MDs, studies reporting change-from-baseline and studies reporting post-intervention values can usually be pooled because, on average in randomized trials, they estimate the same intervention effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to use the appropriate means and SDs for each study; consider placing different outcome types in separate subgroups for clarity though pooling is legitimate. If change scores increase precision, those studies will be weighted more due to smaller SDs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not combine change scores and post-intervention values when using SMD
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-intervention values and change scores should not in principle be combined using SMD because the SDs used for standardization reflect different quantities (between-person variability at a time point vs variation in change scores).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An option is to standardize SMDs using post-intervention SDs rather than change-score SDs to allow combining, but an appropriate standard error for this approach is not established. Consider subgrouping instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of missing SDs for change scores
rubrics_metrics.description: A common problem is that the SD of change scores is not reported; methods for imputation of SDs are available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chapter 6, Section 6.5.2.8 for approaches to impute missing SDs when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider and address skewed continuous data
rubrics_metrics.description: Review authors should consider the possibility and implications of skewed data when analysing continuous outcomes (MECIR Box 10.5.a — Highly desirable). Skewed data may not be well summarized by means and SDs and can mislead in small studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose skew when possible (e.g. (mean - lowest_possible_value)/SD <2 suggests skew; <1 strong evidence). Consider transformation (e.g. log), obtain transformed summaries or IPD, and consult a statistician. Do not mix log-transformed and untransformed data in meta-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix log-transformed and untransformed data
rubrics_metrics.description: Log-transformed and untransformed data should not be combined in a meta-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If trials report results on a log scale (geometric means), perform meta-analysis on the transformed scale or transform data consistently across studies prior to pooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options for combining dichotomous and continuous outcome data
rubrics_metrics.description: When some studies present an outcome as dichotomous and others as continuous, consider summarizing results in several ways (continuous means and SDs, dichotomous counts, or text as 'Other data') or using statistical approaches to re-express effect measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to obtain missing data from investigators. Methods exist to re-express odds ratios as SMDs and vice versa (e.g., Chinn 2000 formulas) under assumptions (logistic distribution, equal variabilities). Convert standard errors appropriately and combine with the generic inverse-variance method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-expression conversions between ORs and SMDs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under assumptions that underlying continuous measurements follow a logistic distribution with equal variability, odds ratios can be re-expressed as SMDs and vice versa using simple constants (√3/π = 0.5513 and π/√3 = 1.814).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply the standard error of log OR by 0.5513 to obtain the SE of SMD, or multiply SMD by 1.814 to get log OR. Combine converted estimates with generic inverse-variance methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of ordinal outcomes and measurement scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinal/scale outcomes are often analysed as dichotomous or continuous depending on original analyses; proportional odds models are an option when the same ordinal scale (few categories) is used across studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proportional odds models can be more efficient than dichotomization but require suitable software and yield a summary measure (proportional odds ratio) that may be hard to interpret. Methods exist to combine related scales with different category definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling counts and rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts are event counts per participant (can be >1); rates are counts per person-time. Rates assume constant underlying risk across participants and time — an assumption that should be assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rate ratios can be combined via log rate ratios with generic inverse-variance or Poisson regression. Consider whether rate analysis is appropriate (e.g., Pearl index often inappropriate). Rate differences are also possible using generic inverse-variance; dichotomization of counts may be an alternative in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches for time-to-event outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Two main approaches: (1) use 'O − E' and 'V' statistics (entered as 'O − E and Variance' in RevMan — only fixed-effect methods available); (2) combine log hazard ratios and SEs (from Cox models) using generic inverse-variance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Log-rank estimates can be converted into log hazard ratios and SEs to allow combination. Choose method based on available extracted data or IPD re-analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish types of heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Heterogeneity is variability among studies and includes clinical diversity (participants/interventions/outcomes), methodological diversity (study design, outcome measurement, risk of bias), and statistical heterogeneity (variation in intervention effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis should only be considered when studies are sufficiently homogeneous in participants, interventions, comparisons and outcomes to yield a clinically meaningful answer (MECIR C62 — Mandatory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess presence and extent of statistical heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether study results are consistent (visual overlap of CIs) and use statistical tests (Chi-squared test) and inconsistency measures (I²) to quantify heterogeneity (MECIR C63 — Mandatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Chi² cautiously (low power with few/small studies; high power with many studies). Avoid relying on simple I² thresholds; consider magnitude/direction of effects and strength of evidence. Uncertainty in I² is substantial with few studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for addressing identified heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: When heterogeneity is present, options include: check data for errors; avoid meta-analysis; explore heterogeneity via pre-specified subgroup analyses or meta-regression; ignore heterogeneity (fixed-effect caveats); use random-effects meta-analysis; reconsider effect measure; or, with caution, exclude outlying studies (perform sensitivity analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations should be pre-specified where possible; exploratory analyses formed after seeing results generate hypotheses only and should be interpreted with caution. Avoid excluding studies solely based on their results; perform sensitivity analyses and report rationale. Take heterogeneity into account in interpretation (MECIR C69 — Mandatory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating heterogeneity using random-effects models
rubrics_metrics.description: Random-effects meta-analysis assumes studies estimate different but related intervention effects following a distribution (commonly normal); it adjusts study standard errors to incorporate between-study variance (τ²).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random-effects models give relatively more weight to smaller studies. The model does not solve heterogeneity; exploring causes is still preferable. The choice of assumed distribution is conventional and its validity is hard to establish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision considerations: fixed-effect versus random-effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-effect assumes a single true intervention effect across studies; random-effects assumes a distribution of effects. Both yield identical results if no heterogeneity. Choice should not be made solely on statistical tests for heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether intervention effects are plausibly identical (favor fixed-effect) or likely to vary (favor random-effects). A pragmatic plan is to perform both and present random-effects if no funnel-plot asymmetry; if asymmetry is present both methods may be problematic. Be aware random-effects gives more weight to small studies and may exacerbate small-study bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of random-effects summary estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The summary estimate and CI from a random-effects meta-analysis refer to the centre (mean) of the distribution of effects and do not describe the width of that distribution (degree of heterogeneity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is inappropriate to quote the random-effects mean and CI in isolation as if they fully describe the meta-analysis; also report measures of heterogeneity and discuss implications.
